text.p: President Fernando Henrique Cardoso, stung by a fresh setback in his drive to reform the government, criticised what he called the "disgraceful" behaviour of Congress, newspapers said on Friday.

"Taking two years to vote on important issues is a disgrace," Cardoso told reporters during an official visit to Canada, which ended on Thursday. "I am going to make an appeal for (lawmakers) to vote. I am going to say: please, vote, vote," he said.

The government was dealt a major blow on Wednesday when left-wing opposition parties in the Chamber of Deputies struck down a central article of a civil service reform bill. The article would have allowed central and local governments to hire workers without offering them jobs-for-life guarantees.
Public sector workers who follow a hiring procedure and serve two years in their posts cannot be fired, making it hard for central and local governments to reduce payroll spending.
The defeat was also the latest in a string of problems to beset the civil service reform bill since it was sent to Congress in August 1995 as a means of cutting public spending.

A proposal to end the job security of public workers was watered down after opposition from within the civil service and a large group of government-allied lawmakers rebelled at the prospect of being included under a pay cap.

The congressmen believed they were entitled to more than the $10,200-per-month ceiling and many of them voted with the opposition to defeat the government on Wednesday. Other amendments seeking to change the civil service reform bill were due to be voted on in the Chamber of Deputies in May.

Brazil's media reacted with outrage to Wednesday's result. "It was a message to the government that without ... mutual back-scratching there will be no reforms. Even if it means the return of inflation ... and the country being stuck in administrative pre-history," Jornal do Brasil said on Friday.

O Globo columnist Tereza Cruvinel said the snail-paced progress of reform had already convinced Cardoso of the need to call an extraordinary "revisory" session of Congress in 1999. Such a session would enable the government to approve changes to the constitution with only a simple majority and not the three-fifths majority normally required.
